title: IX. The Galloping Troika. The End Of The Prosecutor’s Speech.
paragraphs: Ippolit Kirillovitch had chosen the historical method of presentation, the one so beloved by all nervous speakers, who find in its structure a check on their own overeager rhetoric. At this point in his speech he wandered off into a discussion of Grushenka's “first lover,” and offered up several interesting thoughts on the subject.

“Karamazov, who'd been frantically jealous of every man alive, collapsed, so to speak, and simply gave way before this first lover. What makes it stranger still is that he seems to have hardly given this formidable rival a thought. He'd regarded him as a distant danger, and Karamazov always lives in the present moment. He may even have thought of him as something close to fiction. But his wounded heart understood at once that the woman had been hiding this new rival from him, deceiving him, precisely because the man was anything but fiction to her — because he was the one hope of her life. Grasping this instantly, he gave up.”

“Gentlemen of the jury, I can't help lingering on this unexpected trait in the prisoner's character. He suddenly shows an irresistible longing for fairness, a respect for the woman and a recognition of her right to love — and all this at the very moment when he'd stained his hands with his father's blood for her sake! True, that spilled blood was already crying out for vengeance, because, having ruined his soul and his life in this world, he was forced at that same instant to ask himself what he was, and what he could possibly still be, to her — to that being dearer to him than his own soul — measured against that former lover who had come back, penitent, full of renewed love, to the woman he had once betrayed, bringing honorable proposals and the promise of a reformed, happy life. And what, unlucky man that he was, could he offer her now? What did he have left to give?”

“Karamazov felt all this, knew every path was closed to him by his crime, that he was already a condemned man and not one with a future ahead of him! This thought crushed him. And so he instantly seized on one frantic plan, which, to a man of Karamazov's temperament, must have seemed the only possible way out of his terrible situation. That way out was suicide. He ran for the pistols he'd left in pawn with his friend Perhotin, and on the way, as he ran, he pulled from his pocket the very money for which he'd stained his hands with his father's blood. Oh, now he needed money more than ever. Karamazov was going to die, Karamazov was going to shoot himself — and it would be remembered! To be sure, he was a poet, and had burned the candle at both ends all his life. ‘To her, to her! And there — oh, there I'll throw a feast for the whole world, the likes of which has never been seen, one that will be remembered and talked about for years! In the middle of shouts of wild merriment, reckless gypsy songs and dancing, I'll raise my glass and drink to the woman I adore and to her newfound happiness! And then, right there, at her feet, I'll blow my brains out in front of her and punish myself! She'll remember Mitya Karamazov sometimes — she'll see how Mitya loved her, she'll feel for Mitya!’”

“Here we see, in excess, a taste for grand gestures, romantic despair, sentimentality, and the wild recklessness of the Karamazovs. Yes — but there's something else, gentlemen of the jury, something that cries out in the soul, throbs ceaselessly in the mind, and poisons the heart to the point of death — that something is conscience, gentlemen of the jury, its verdict, its terrible torments! The pistol will settle everything — the pistol is the only way out! But beyond — I don't know whether Karamazov, at that moment, wondered ‘what lies beyond,’ whether Karamazov could, like Hamlet, wonder ‘what lies beyond.’ No, gentlemen of the jury — they have their Hamlets, but we still have only our Karamazovs!”

Here Ippolit Kirillovitch painted a detailed picture of Mitya's preparations — the scene at Perhotin's, at the shop, with the drivers. He quoted numerous words and actions, all confirmed by witnesses, and the picture made a terrible impression on the audience. The guilt of this harried, desperate man stood out clear and convincing once all the facts were laid side by side.

“What need did he have for caution? Two or three times he very nearly confessed, hinted at it, all but came out and said it.” (Then followed the testimony given by witnesses.) “He even shouted at the peasant driving him, ‘Do you know you're driving a murderer!’ But it was impossible for him to come out and say it — he had to reach Mokroe and finish his romance there. But what was waiting for the unlucky man? Almost from the first minute at Mokroe he saw that his invincible rival was perhaps nothing of the kind, that the toast to their newfound happiness was neither wanted nor welcome. But you already know the facts, gentlemen of the jury, from the preliminary inquiry. Karamazov's triumph over his rival was total, and his soul passed into an entirely new phase — perhaps the most terrible phase his soul has ever passed through, or ever will.”

“One can say with certainty, gentlemen of the jury,” the prosecutor went on, “that outraged nature and a guilty heart exact their own vengeance more thoroughly than any earthly justice ever could. What's more, justice and punishment here on earth actually ease the punishment of nature, and are indeed essential to the criminal soul in such moments, as its rescue from despair. Because I can't even imagine the horror, the moral agony, Karamazov must have felt on learning that she loved him — that for his sake she had turned away her first lover, that she was calling him, Mitya, to a new life, promising him happiness — and when? When it was all over for him, when nothing was possible anymore!”

“By the way, I'll note in passing a point of some importance, for the light it throws on the prisoner's state of mind at the time. This woman, the object of his love, had been, right up until the last moment — right up to the instant of his arrest — a being unattainable, passionately desired, and out of reach. Yet why didn't he shoot himself then? Why did he abandon his plan, and even forget where his pistol was? It was precisely that passionate longing for love, and the hope of finally satisfying it, that held him back. All through the revels he stayed close beside his adored mistress, who was there at the feast with him and more charming, more captivating to him than ever — he never left her side, abasing himself before her in worship.”

“His passion might well, for a moment, have stifled not only his fear of arrest but even the torments of conscience. For a moment — oh, only for a moment! I can picture the state of mind of a criminal hopelessly enslaved by these forces — first, the influence of drink, of noise and excitement, of the thud of the dancing and the wail of the singing, and of her, flushed with wine, singing and dancing and laughing at him! Second, the lingering hope that the fatal reckoning might still be far off — that they wouldn't come for him until the next morning at the very earliest. So he had a few hours, and that's a great deal — a very great deal! In a few hours a man can think of many things. I imagine he felt something like what condemned men feel on their way to the scaffold. There's still a long, long street left to cross, walking at a measured pace, past thousands of people. Then there'll be a turn into another street, and only at the far end of that one, the dreaded place of execution! I fancy that at the start of the journey, the condemned man, sitting on his cart of shame, must feel he still has a whole lifetime ahead of him. The houses fall away behind, the cart rolls on — oh, that's nothing, there's still a long way to the turn into the second street, and he still looks boldly to right and left at those thousands of coldly curious people with their eyes fixed on him, and still imagines he's just such a man as they are. But now comes the turn into the next street. Oh, that's nothing, nothing — there's still a whole street ahead of him, and however many houses he's passed already, he'll still believe plenty remain. And so on, all the way to the very scaffold.”

“This, I imagine, is how it was with Karamazov then. ‘They haven't had time yet,’ he must have thought. ‘I might still find a way out — oh, there's still time to think of some defense, and right now, right now — she's so captivating!’”

“His soul was in turmoil and dread, and yet he still managed to set aside half his money and hide it somewhere — I can find no other explanation for the disappearance of fully half the three thousand he'd just taken from under his father's pillow. He'd been to Mokroe more than once before, had spent two whole days carousing there already, and knew every passage and outbuilding of the big old house. My guess is that part of the money was hidden somewhere in that house, not long before his arrest — in some crevice, under some floorboard, in some corner, under the roof. To what end, I'll be asked? Well — the catastrophe might strike at any moment, of course; he hadn't yet worked out how to face it, hadn't had the time, his head was pounding and his heart was with her — but money, money was essential no matter what. With money, a man is always still a man. Perhaps such foresight, at such a moment, strikes you as unnatural? But he assures us himself that a month earlier, at a tense and critical moment, he'd halved his money and sewn it into a little bag. And though that wasn't true, as we'll prove directly, it shows the idea was a familiar one to Karamazov — he'd already considered it. What's more, when he declared at the inquiry that he'd put fifteen hundred roubles in a bag (a bag that never existed), he may well have invented that little bag on the spur of the moment, precisely because two hours earlier he actually had divided his money and hidden half of it at Mokroe until morning, in case of emergency, simply so as not to be carrying it on him. Two extremes, gentlemen of the jury — remember that a Karamazov can hold two extremes in mind at once, and both together.”

“We searched the house, but found no money. It may still be there, or it may have vanished the next day and be in the prisoner's hands even now. In any case, he was at her side, on his knees before her — she lay on the bed, he stretched his hands out to her, and he had so completely forgotten everything else that he didn't even hear the men come to arrest him. He hadn't had time to prepare any line of defense. He was caught off guard, unprepared, and brought face to face with his judges, the arbiters of his fate.”

“Gentlemen of the jury, there are moments in the carrying out of our duties when it's a terrible thing to face a man — terrible for him too. The moments of watching that animal fear, when the criminal sees that everything is lost, but still struggles, still means to go on struggling, when every instinct of self-preservation rises up in him at once and he looks at you with pleading, suffering eyes, studying you, your face, your thoughts, unsure which way you'll strike, his distracted mind spinning out a thousand plans in an instant, and yet still afraid to speak, afraid of giving himself away! This purgatory of the spirit, this animal thirst for self-preservation, these humiliating moments of the human soul, are terrible to watch, and can rouse horror and pity for the criminal even in a lawyer. And this is exactly what we all witnessed that night.”

“At first he was thunderstruck, and in his terror let slip a few deeply incriminating words. ‘Blood! I've earned it!’ But he quickly caught himself. He hadn't prepared what he was going to say, what answer he'd give — he had nothing ready but a flat denial. ‘I'm not guilty of my father's death.’ That was his line of defense for the moment, and behind it he hoped to throw up some sort of barricade. His first damaging outbursts he hurried to explain away, insisting he was responsible only for the servant Grigory's death. ‘For that bloodshed, yes, I'm guilty — but who killed my father, gentlemen, who killed him? Who could have killed him, if not I?’ Do you hear that — he asked us that, us, the very people who'd come to ask him that question! Do you hear that phrase, blurted out with such premature haste — ‘if not I’ — the animal cunning in it, the naïveté, the Karamazov impatience? ‘I didn't kill him, and you mustn't think I did! I wanted to kill him, gentlemen, I wanted to,’ he rushes to admit (he was in a hurry, a terrible hurry), ‘but still, I'm not guilty — it wasn't I who murdered him.’ He concedes to us that he wanted to murder him, as if to say: you see for yourselves how truthful I am, so you'll believe all the more readily that I didn't murder him. Oh, in such cases the criminal is often astonishingly shallow and credulous.”

“At that point one of the lawyers asked him, almost casually, the simplest possible question: ‘Wasn't it Smerdyakov who killed him?’ Then, just as we expected, he grew furious that we'd anticipated him and caught him off guard, before he'd had time to prepare his ground, to pick and choose the moment when it would seem most natural to bring Smerdyakov's name up. He immediately swung to the opposite extreme, as he always does, and began insisting that Smerdyakov couldn't have killed him, wasn't capable of it. But don't believe him — that was only his cunning; he hadn't really given up on Smerdyakov at all; on the contrary, he meant to bring him forward again, because he had no one else to offer, but he'd do it later, since for the moment that line had been spoiled for him. He'd bring him up, perhaps, the next day, or even some days later, waiting for the right moment to cry out to us, ‘You know, I was more skeptical about Smerdyakov than any of you — you remember that yourselves — but now I'm convinced. He killed him, he must have!’ And for the time being he falls back on a sullen, irritable denial. Impatience and anger, though, drove him into the most clumsy, incredible explanation of how he'd looked in at his father's window and then respectfully withdrawn. The worst of it was that he didn't yet know how things stood — didn't know what Grigory had testified.”

“We proceeded to search him. The search angered him, but also, oddly, encouraged him — the full three thousand wasn't found on him, only half of it. And no doubt it was precisely in that moment of angry silence that the fiction of the little bag first occurred to him. No doubt he was aware himself of how implausible the story sounded, and struggled painfully to make it more convincing, to weave it into a plausible-sounding tale. In cases like this, the first duty, the chief task of the examining lawyers, is to keep the criminal from preparing himself — to catch him off guard, so that he blurts out his cherished ideas in all their raw simplicity, improbability, and inconsistency. The only way to get a criminal talking is through the sudden, apparently offhand disclosure of some new fact, some circumstance of real importance to the case, one he had no idea of and couldn't have foreseen. We had just such a fact ready — Grigory's testimony about the open door the prisoner had run out through. He had completely forgotten about that door, hadn't even suspected Grigory could have seen it.”

“The effect was extraordinary. He leapt up and shouted at us, ‘Then it was Smerdyakov who murdered him — it was Smerdyakov!’ — and in doing so gave away the very defense he'd been holding in reserve, and gave it away in its most implausible form, since Smerdyakov could only have committed the murder after the prisoner had already knocked Grigory down and fled. When we told him that Grigory had seen the door open before he fell, and had heard Smerdyakov behind the screen as he came out of his bedroom, Karamazov was utterly crushed. My esteemed and witty colleague, Nikolay Parfenovitch, told me afterward that he was almost moved to tears at the sight of him. And to make matters worse, the prisoner hurried to tell us about the now-famous little bag — very well, then, you shall hear this romance!”

“Gentlemen of the jury, I've already told you why I consider this romance not merely absurd, but the single most improbable invention that could possibly have been put forward under the circumstances. If you tried, for a bet, to invent the least believable story imaginable, you'd have a hard time finding anything more incredible. The trouble with such stories is that the storytellers, so pleased with themselves, are always tripped up and undone by exactly the details in which real life is so rich, and which these unlucky, involuntary novelists overlook as insignificant trifles. Oh, they have no attention to spare for such details — their minds are fixed on their grand invention as a whole, and imagine anyone daring to pull them up over something so small! But that's precisely how they're caught. The prisoner was asked: ‘Where did you get the material for your little bag, and who sewed it?’ ‘I made it myself.’ ‘And where did you get the linen?’ The prisoner was actually offended — he found it almost insulting to be asked such a trivial question, and, believe it or not, his resentment was genuine! But they're all like that. ‘I tore it off my shirt.’ ‘Then we'll find that shirt among your linen tomorrow, with a piece torn off it.’ And just imagine, gentlemen of the jury, if we really had found that torn shirt (and how could we possibly have failed to, in his chest of drawers or his trunk?) — that would have been a fact, a solid fact supporting his account! But he was incapable of that kind of reflection. ‘I don't remember — maybe it wasn't off my shirt. I sewed it into one of my landlady's caps.’ ‘What kind of cap?’ ‘It was an old cotton rag of hers, lying around.’ ‘And you remember that clearly?’ ‘No, I don't.’ And he was angry, very angry — and yet, imagine, not remembering it! At the most terrible moments of a man's life — say, when he's being led to execution — he remembers precisely such trifles. He'll forget everything except some green roof flashing past on the road, or a jackdaw perched on a cross — that he'll remember. He hid the making of that little bag from his household; he must have remembered his humiliating fear that someone might come in and find him with a needle in his hand, how at the slightest sound he'd duck behind the screen (there is a screen in his lodgings).”

“But, gentlemen of the jury, why am I telling you all this — all these details, these trifles?” Ippolit Kirillovitch suddenly cried. “Simply because the prisoner still clings to these absurdities to this very moment. He hasn't explained a single thing since that fatal night two months ago; he hasn't added one genuinely illuminating fact to his earlier fantastic claims — it's all trivialities. ‘You must take my word of honor for it.’ Oh, we'd be glad to believe it — eager to believe it, even on his word of honor alone! Are we jackals, thirsting for human blood? Show us a single fact in the prisoner's favor and we'll rejoice — but let it be a solid, real fact, not some inference drawn by his own brother from the look on his face, or from the idea that when he beat his chest he must have meant to point at the little bag, and in the dark, no less. We'll welcome any new fact — we'll be the first to withdraw our charge, we'll hurry to withdraw it. But as things stand, justice cries out, and we hold firm — we can withdraw nothing.”

Ippolit Kirillovitch moved into his final peroration. He looked feverish; he spoke of the blood crying out for vengeance, the blood of a father murdered by his own son for the base motive of robbery! He pointed to the tragic, glaring consistency of the facts.

“And whatever you may hear from the talented, celebrated counsel for the defense,” Ippolit Kirillovitch couldn't resist adding, “whatever eloquent, moving appeals may be made to your feelings, remember that at this moment you stand in a temple of justice. Remember that you are the champions of our justice, the champions of our holy Russia, of her principles, her family, everything she holds sacred! Yes — at this moment you stand here for Russia, and your verdict will echo not only through this hall but across the whole of Russia, and all Russia will hear you as her champions and her judges, and she will take heart or lose heart according to your verdict. Do not disappoint Russia and her hopes. Our fatal troika races on in its headlong flight, perhaps toward destruction, and for a long time now, throughout Russia, men have stretched out imploring hands, calling for a halt to its furious, reckless course. And if other nations step aside from that troika, it may not be out of respect, as the poet would have us believe, but simply out of horror — of horror, perhaps of disgust. And it's well that they step aside; but perhaps one day they will stop doing so, and will form a solid wall against the rushing apparition, and will check the frenzied rush of our lawlessness, for the sake of their own safety, their own enlightenment, their own civilization. Already we hear voices of alarm coming from Europe — they're already beginning to sound. Do not tempt them! Do not add to their growing hatred with a verdict that justifies a son murdering his father!”

Though Ippolit Kirillovitch was genuinely moved, he closed his speech with this rhetorical flourish, and its effect on the audience was extraordinary. When he'd finished, he hurried out and, as I've already mentioned, very nearly fainted in the next room. There was no applause in the courtroom, but the more serious-minded people were pleased. The ladies were less satisfied, though even they admired his eloquence, especially since they felt no real anxiety about the trial's outcome and had full confidence in Fetyukovitch. ‘He'll speak at last, and of course he'll carry everything before him.’

Everyone was looking at Mitya; he sat silent through the whole of the prosecutor's speech, teeth clenched, hands clasped, head bowed. Only now and then he raised his head to listen, especially whenever Grushenka was mentioned. When the prosecutor brought up Rakitin's opinion of her, a look of contempt and anger crossed his face, and he muttered, quite audibly, ‘The Bernards!’ When Ippolit Kirillovitch described how he'd been questioned and tormented at Mokroe, Mitya raised his head and listened with fierce curiosity. At one point he looked ready to jump up and shout something, but he controlled himself and only shrugged his shoulders in disdain. People talked afterward about the end of the speech, about the prosecutor's feat of cross-examining the prisoner at Mokroe, and made fun of Ippolit Kirillovitch. ‘The man couldn't help boasting about his own cleverness,’ they said.
The court adjourned, but only for a short break — a quarter of an hour, twenty minutes at most. There was a buzz of conversation and exclamations throughout the audience. I remember a few of them.
“A weighty speech,” a gentleman in one group observed gravely.
“He brought in too much psychology,” said another voice.
“But it was all true — the plain truth!”
“Yes, he's first-rate at that.”
“He summed it all up.”
“Yes, he summed us up too,” chimed in another voice. “Do you remember, right at the start of his speech, making it sound like we're all like Fyodor Pavlovitch?”
“And at the end, too. But that was all nonsense.”
“And obscure, too.”
“He got a little carried away.”
“It's unfair — it's unfair.”
“No, it was cleverly done, all the same. He's had to wait a long time, but he's had his say — ha ha!”
“What will the counsel for the defense say?”
In another group I overheard:
“He shouldn't have taken a jab at the Petersburg man like that — ‘appealing to your sensibilities,’ do you remember?”
“Yes, that was clumsy of him.”
“He was in too much of a hurry.”
“He's a nervous man.”
“We laugh, but what must the prisoner be feeling right now?”
“Yes — what must it be like for Mitya?”
In a third group:
“Who's that lady, the heavyset one with the lorgnette, sitting at the end?”
“A general's wife, divorced — I know her.”
“That's why she has the lorgnette.”
“She's not much to look at.”
“Oh, no — she's quite a piquant little woman.”
“Two seats past her there's a small fair-haired woman — she's prettier.”
“They caught him neatly at Mokroe, didn't they, eh?”
“Oh, it was clever enough. We've heard it all before — how many times has he told the story at people's houses!”
“And he couldn't resist doing it again now. That's vanity.”
“He's a man with a grievance, heh heh!”
“Yes, and quick to take offense. And too much rhetoric — such long sentences.”
“Yes, he's trying to scare us, he kept trying to scare us. Do you remember that bit about the troika? Something like, ‘They have Hamlets, but so far we only have Karamazovs!’ That was clever, that.”
“That was to win over the liberals. He's afraid of them.”
“Yes, and he's afraid of the lawyer too.”
“Yes — what will Fetyukovitch say?”
“Whatever he says, he won't win over our peasants.”
“You don't think so?”
A fourth group:
“That bit he said about the troika was good — that part about the other nations.”
“And it was true, what he said about other nations not putting up with it.”
“What do you mean?”

“Well — a member of the English Parliament got up last week, talking about the Nihilists, and asked the ministry whether it wasn't high time to step in, to civilize this barbarous people. Ippolit had him in mind, I know he did. He was talking about it just last week.”
“Not an easy job.”
“Not an easy job? Why not?”
“Well, we'd close off Kronstadt and cut off their grain. Where would they get it from?”
“From America. They get it from America now.”
“Nonsense!”
But the bell rang, and everyone rushed back to their seats. Fetyukovitch mounted the tribune.
